title: Sirhind, 1764
hookLine: the Dal Khalsa took Sirhind and the land of Punjab passed to the Sikh confederacies

lines: THE WALL WHERE THE SAHIBZADE DIED.
THE DAL KHALSA AT THE GATES AGAIN.
cards: Sirhind. This path has stood here before. Once in grief, at the wall where the Guru's youngest sons were put to death on the governor's order.
And once with Banda Singh Bahadur's forces, who took the city years later. Then the city passed out of Sikh hands again, and the hard decades you've been hearing about came down.
Now the riders of the Dal Khalsa are outside its walls once more.

teach.b: The story comes in three movements. First, the taking. Tradition says the bands of the Dal Khalsa came together against Sirhind and defeated its governor, who was killed in the fighting.
For Sikhs, this wasn't just another town on the map. It was the place their memory kept circling back to. Second, what they did with the city.

teach.h: A BRICK THROWN IN THE RIVER.
teach.b: Tradition says Sikhs treated Sirhind as a place under a shadow, and that for a long time Sikhs passing by would take a brick from its ruins and throw it in the river.
Some tellings call it the city the Guru's curse fell on. And at the spot where the young Sahibzade died, Sikhs marked the ground; a gurdwara called Fatehgarh Sahib stands there now.

teach.h: FATEHGARH: FATEH SINGH'S NAME, A WORD FOR VICTORY.
teach.b: Its name carries the name of the younger of the two, Fateh Singh, and fateh means victory. The place of the children's deaths bears a word for victory.

teach.h: THE LAND PASSES TO THE MISLS.
teach.b: Third, the land. After Sirhind, the territory around it was divided among the Sikh confederacies, the misls, each band holding its own share.
In this telling, the chiefs stop being hunted riders and start holding the countryside. Bands who had once hidden in forests and deserts now held the villages.
That's the turn, and nothing about the hard decades had promised it. The persecutions, the great killing, the temple blown up: people at Sirhind remembered all of it.
And here, at the city where the smallest martyrs died, the tide turned.

how: Sikhs remember the fall of Sirhind in Sikh histories, and gather at Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib, where the younger Sahibzade died, to remember them.

games.q: you ride with the Dal Khalsa into Sirhind, the city where the Guru's youngest sons were killed. the governor is dead. what do you do with the spot where the children died?
o: leave it alone and forget it.
mark it, so the children are remembered there.
games.why: Sikhs marked it, and the gurdwara there is called Fatehgarh Sahib, carrying Fateh Singh's name. fateh means victory.

practice: Look back over your own life and find one moment when something changed direction: a phone call, a door that opened, a day you stopped doing something, or started.
It may not have looked like much at the time; hold it in mind, and notice what came before it, and how long the before lasted. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Sirhind. The city of the Sahibzade's deaths, taken by the Dal Khalsa, after which the land passed to the misls. This week: Baba Deep Singh, the pool filled in, captives home, Kup Rahira, the temple destroyed, Diwali at the ruins, and Sirhind. Today's word.
